questions.stem: Who runs a tool after the model returns a tool call?

options.A: The language model runs it during its own inference process
options.B: Your application code runs it, or can refuse to run it
options.C: The vector database runs it before any answer is written
options.D: The embedding service runs it whenever text is retrieved

questions.rationale: The model only returns a request. Your application decides whether to execute that request.

questions.stem: Which three limits do tools help a language model overcome?

options.A: Long context windows, image input, and spoken replies
options.B: Spelling mistakes, weak grammar, and formatting issues
options.C: Live data access, outside actions, and unreliable math
options.D: Document chunking, embeddings, and vector database size

questions.rationale: Day 3 shows that the model cannot fetch live data, take outside actions, or do reliable arithmetic. Tools fix those by letting the model ask and your code do the work.

questions.stem: What is an agent in the Day 3 tool loop?

options.A: A larger model that needs no function schema at all
options.B: A fixed script that always calls every available tool
options.C: A search index that stores completed tool results forever
options.D: A bounded request-execute-return loop with a clear goal

questions.rationale: An agent is the tool loop given a goal and a limit on how many times it may repeat.

questions.stem: Why is a vague tool description such as "Gets leave data" a problem?

options.A: The model lacks clear timing, scope, and call exclusions
options.B: JSON Schema rejects descriptions shorter than one full page
options.C: Vector stores cannot store tool text written in plain English
options.D: Models can only call tools when their description field is empty

questions.rationale: The description is what the model reads to decide when to call a tool. A vague description leads to guessing and over-calling.

questions.stem: Why does every agent need a step cap?

options.A: GPUs reject more than one tool request by hardware design
options.B: Free tiers always block long loops before any cost appears
options.C: A failed goal can repeat paid calls while history grows
options.D: Models forget earlier tool results after exactly five steps

questions.rationale: Without a cap, an unsatisfiable goal can keep requesting tools. Each step is a paid call, and growing history makes later steps more expensive.

questions.stem: Why should an agent look up tools with an allow-list dictionary?

options.A: So the model can invent brand-new tool names during runtime
options.B: So only approved functions can run from a requested name
options.C: So every completed tool response is stored as an embedding
options.D: So the agent can skip every check on argument types forever

questions.rationale: Using an allow-list keeps execution on an approved set of functions. Blind dispatch on a model-supplied name is unsafe.

questions.stem: How should a tool report failure so the agent can recover?

options.A: Raise an exception that ends the process with no message
options.B: Return an empty string and hope the model fills the gap
options.C: Remove the tool from the allow-list after the first miss
options.D: Return a readable error the model can use to adjust

questions.rationale: Error messages are prompts for the model. A readable error lets the loop recover instead of crashing or inventing.

questions.stem: How does agentic RAG differ from plain RAG?

options.A: Plain RAG retrieves once; agentic RAG decides whether to search
options.B: Plain RAG never retrieves; agentic RAG retrieves only one passage
options.C: Agentic RAG deletes the retriever and trains a model each turn
options.D: Agentic RAG removes citations so the final answer can stay short

questions.rationale: In agentic RAG, retrieval is a tool among several. The model chooses whether to search, what to search for, and whether the result is good enough.

questions.stem: When should an agent pause for human approval before acting?

options.A: When the next search term depends on the last result
options.B: When answer quality matters more than latency or cost
options.C: When the planned action cannot be undone after it runs
options.D: When several specialist models could answer similar tasks

questions.rationale: Human-in-the-loop is for irreversible actions such as money, messages, or deletions. The other cases map to ReAct, reflection, and routing.

questions.stem: When should you avoid building an agent and use a fixed sequence instead?

options.A: When several tools are needed and you cannot know which one
options.B: When the path never changes and a script can be tested
options.C: When the next step depends on what the last step returned
options.D: When the system must recover from partial failure alone

questions.rationale: If the path never changes, a script is clearer and easier to test. Build an agent only when the next step depends on intermediate results.
